title: Marine Biology
short: The biology of organisms and biological processes in oceans, coasts, estuaries, and other marine environments.
bigPicture: Marine biology is defined mainly by the environment and organisms being studied, not by one single method. A marine biologist might investigate whale communication, fish physiology, coral disease, plankton food webs, or how coastal development changes an estuary. The field therefore overlaps with behavior, physiology, ecology, genetics, conservation, and zoology. It remains useful context, but marine specialization does not drive the current school recommendations.

starterResources.title: NOAA National Marine Sanctuaries — Student Resources

terms.definition: The study of interactions among marine organisms and their physical environment.
The study of biological processes in the ocean, often at large spatial scales and closely connected to ocean chemistry and physics.
A coastal system where freshwater and seawater mix, creating highly variable conditions and productive habitats.
Open-water habitats away from the seafloor or shoreline.
Habitats on or closely associated with the seafloor.
How organisms maintain the right balance of water and salts in their bodies.

focus.title: Marine animals and organismal biology
focus.description: How fishes, marine mammals, invertebrates, reptiles, seabirds, and other organisms function, reproduce, develop, and survive in marine conditions.
focus.source: NOAA National Marine Sanctuaries: Student Resources

focus.title: Behavior and movement
focus.description: Migration, communication, social behavior, foraging, navigation, and responses to changing ocean conditions.

focus.title: Marine ecology and food webs
focus.description: How species interact with predators, prey, competitors, habitats, and physical processes from reefs and estuaries to the open ocean.

focus.title: Physiological adaptation
focus.description: How animals manage salinity, pressure, oxygen, temperature, diving, and other demands that differ sharply from terrestrial environments.

questions.question: How do marine animals navigate, communicate, or migrate?
questions.approach: Through tagging, acoustic recording, visual surveys, behavioral observation, and environmental data.

questions.question: How does changing temperature or ocean chemistry affect an animal?
questions.approach: With controlled physiology experiments, field monitoring, or long-term datasets linking biological responses to environmental conditions.

questions.question: Why is a fish, coral, or invertebrate population changing?
questions.approach: By combining surveys, life-history data, food-web information, disease observations, fishing pressure, and habitat conditions.

questions.question: How are estuarine and coastal animals affected by freshwater input and development?
questions.approach: By sampling organisms and environmental conditions across salinity, nutrient, pollution, and habitat gradients.

questions.question: What can animal movement reveal about habitat needs?
questions.approach: By pairing telemetry or photo-identification with oceanographic and habitat data.

questions.question: How do marine species cope with extreme physical conditions?
questions.approach: By measuring respiration, metabolism, osmoregulation, temperature tolerance, or diving physiology.

responsibilities: Conduct field, vessel, laboratory, aquarium, or remote-monitoring studies.
Identify organisms and collect biological and environmental measurements.
Analyze movement, behavior, physiology, population, or ecological data.
Maintain careful field records, permits, samples, and research documentation.
knowledgeSkills: Oceanographic context relevant to the biological question

variations.label: The environment defines the field
variations.description: Marine biology can be behavior, physiology, genetics, ecology, or conservation carried out with marine organisms or systems.

variations.label: Not all work is underwater
variations.description: Many marine biologists spend more time in laboratories, on boats, at computers, or analyzing samples than diving.

variations.label: Coastal boundaries are porous
variations.description: Estuaries and species that move between fresh and salt water are normal parts of marine research, so a strict saltwater-only boundary is misleading.

variations.label: Job titles are often more specific
variations.description: Positions may be advertised as fisheries biologist, marine mammal researcher, aquarist, ecologist, research technician, or a taxon specialty instead of simply marine biologist.

settings: Coastal field stations, research vessels, and conservation organizations
realities: Marine biology is broad enough that the day-to-day work depends more on the specialty than on the word marine.
Field seasons, boat work, weather, and remote locations can shape some jobs, while others are primarily laboratory or analytical.
Quantitative skills and scientific writing matter across nearly every marine specialty.
Independent research positions commonly require graduate education.
A marine label is not automatically a better fit for someone interested in animals; the actual coursework in behavior, physiology, zoology, and hands-on work matters more.
